Nestlings of the Round-tailed manakin (Ceratopipra chloromeros) hatch at a remarkably small size, with a neonatal body mass of just 1.8 grams [Wwb = 1.8 grams]. This altricial chick, entirely dependent on parental provisioning for warmth and food, undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain to reach an asymptotic adult body mass of 16.5 grams [Wwi = 16.5 grams]. The incubation period is relatively brief; field observations of active nests indicate that eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] produce hatchlings after approximately 17 days [ab = approximately 17 days]. This developmental duration is typical for small-bodied passerines and reflects the constrained thermal regime of the nest microclimate within the humid montane forests of southeastern Peru and Bolivia. The 17-day incubation period, measured under natural nest temperatures averaging 34 °C, contrasts with the shorter developmental times observed in more open-country congeners, suggesting that the cooler, shaded understory habitat of this manakin species may impose a slight lengthening of the embryonic period. The combination of a low birth mass and a rapid postnatal growth trajectory is characteristic of manakins and other frugivorous suboscines.

In a series of controlled respirometry trials conducted on adult male Round-tailed manakins, the resting metabolic rate was quantified at a physiological temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The measured basal oxygen consumption was 52.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 52.73 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with the elevated metabolic demands typical of the intensely active lekking display behavior observed in this genus at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This mass-specific metabolic rate underscores the high energetic cost of maintaining the endothermic physiology required for sustained aerial and courtship performances. The measurements, taken from post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, provide a reliable baseline for understanding the daily energetic budgets of breeding males that must allocate substantial resources to both self-maintenance and territory defense. Comparative data from related Pipridae species suggest that this magnitude of oxygen consumption is consistent with the high-frequency wing whirring sounds produced during mechanical display elements.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the life history milestones follow a distinct ontogenetic schedule. Sexual maturity is attained at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching], a relatively brief juvenile period for a bird of this ultimate size at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The fledgling stage, defined as the achievement of independent flight from the nest, occurs even earlier, at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching], a typical value for altricial Passeriformes at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. The rapid progression from hatching to flight capability reflects the intense predation pressure faced by nestlings in the understory environment. These developmental timings indicate that the species employs a fast-paced early life history strategy, channeling resources into somatic growth and neuromuscular maturation to minimize the vulnerable nest-bound period. This contrasts with the slower maturation rates observed in larger-bodied forest frugivores.

The first successful reproduction event, or the initiation of an individual's first brood, occurs at 438 days after hatching [tR = 438 days after hatching] at an active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This interval to first breeding is a markedly long pre-reproductive phase for a 16.5 gram [Wwi = 16.5 gram] passerine. The delay is not attributable to slow somatic growth but rather to the prolonged period required by males to establish and defend a high-quality lekking territory within a competitive social hierarchy. Females likely undergo a similar or slightly shorter deferral as they assess territory quality and male display prowess. This first brood timing is a critical demographic parameter that shapes the generation time and population turnover rate of this species. The long wait to first reproduction is a classic feature of a slow life-history strategy, offset by a relatively extended reproductive lifespan.

The maximum recorded longevity for the Round-tailed manakin, observed under natural field conditions at an active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], is approximately 9.8 years [am = approximately 9.8 years]. This lifespan is substantial for a passerine of only 16.5 grams [Wwi = 16.5 grams] and indicates a life-history strategy characterized by high adult survival. Over the course of this extended life, females produce a maximum of 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], and the annual reproductive output is constrained by a single nesting attempt per year [F_R_i = single nesting attempt per year], a low frequency typical of tropical frugivores. This combined annual output of approximately 2 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 2 offspring per year], measured at 41.8 °C, results in a modest yearly fecundity that depends crucially on the ability of adults to survive multiple breeding seasons. The combination of a small clutch size, infrequent nesting, and a long lifespan underscores a slow-paced life history finely tuned to the predictable but low-resource environment of the Andean foothill forests.
